title: YMnotes Digestive System — After Mid-Module Extras

part_a.title: After Mid-Module Chapters
part_a.intro: Additions for the chapters in the second half of your book, in book order. Chapter 15 starts in the first-half file (p. 195) and continues into the second-half file, so it is included here in full.

chapters.title: Colorectal Cancer
chapters.files_note: Split chapter: pp. 195–197 are in the first-half file (PDF pp. 198–200); pp. 197–209 are in the second-half file (PDF pp. 1–13). Page 197 appears in both.

items.head: Adenocarcinoma: 98% of large-bowel cancers
text: Your book says “more than 90%” of colorectal carcinomas are adenocarcinomas. GIT Others gives a precise figure: 98% of all cancers of the large intestine are adenocarcinomas.

items.head: Two kinds of mucoid (mucinous) carcinoma
list: Mucinous adenocarcinoma: abundant extracellular mucin (your book: >50% mucinous material).
Signet ring cell carcinoma: the mucin stays inside the malignant cell and pushes the nucleus to one side (eccentric nucleus).

items.head: Add irradiation to the predisposing factors
text: GIT Others lists irradiation as a predisposing factor for colorectal adenocarcinoma, along with adenoma, familial polyposis, IBD and gene mutations. It is not in your book’s list.

items.head: Age at presentation: 50–70 or 60–79 years?
list: GIT Others p. 19: “Age of 50–70 years.”
GIT Others p. 20 and your book Ch 4 p. 74: “between 60 and 79 years of age”.
Your book Ch 15 p. 196: “old age, however no age is immune”.
items.after: GIT Others contradicts itself. Ask your teacher which range to learn.

chapters.title: Pyogenic Liver Abscess
chapters.files_note: Second-half file, PDF pp. 128–135. The amoebic liver abscess section is on pp. 329–331.

items.head: Blood count in amoebic liver abscess
list: Your book Ch 25 p. 331: “CBC: Leukocytosis and eosinophilia”.

GIT Others p. 47, and your book Ch 9 p. 138: CBC shows polymorphonuclear leucocytosis, which helps separate amoebic liver abscess from viral hepatitis. Neither mentions eosinophilia for amoebic liver abscess.
items.after: Both agree on leucocytosis. Check with your teacher whether eosinophilia should be learned.

checked_none: Leptospirosis and yellow fever liver involvement is already in Ch 7 (pp. 113–114).
Hepatosplenic schistosomiasis is already on p. 283 and in Ch 9.
Schistosomal periportal fibrosis (p. 310) and PPIs for bleeding varices (Ch 3 p. 47) are already covered.
GIT Others only names hydatid disease as a differential of amoebic liver abscess, which Ch 9 already does.
Biliary Ascaris is already on p. 390; the Ascaris details in GIT Others are all in Ch 9.

part_b.title: Earlier-Chapter Additions Found in GIT Others
part_b.intro: Most of GIT Others covers chapters from the first half of your book (before the mid-module). These points are missing from those chapters. They are kept separate from Part A and follow your book’s chapter numbers. Use them when revising the earlier chapters.

chapters.title: The Stomach and Duodenum
chapters.files_note: First-half file, PDF pp. 36–72. GIT Others pp. 1–6 (drug treatment of gastritis and peptic ulcer) repeat your book’s pp. 44–50 almost word for word.

items.fits: Pharmacology → 1. Proton Pump Inhibitors → Adverse effects
items.head: Long-term PPI use and bone
text: Osteoporosis is a possible complication of chronic (long-term) PPI use. Add it to the PPI adverse effects, after vitamin B12 deficiency.

items.head: Misoprostol: PGE1 or PGE2 analogue?
list: Your book p. 37: “a synthetic prostaglandin E₂ analogue”.
Your book p. 48 and GIT Others p. 4: “Synthetic PGE1 analog”.
items.after: Your two pages disagree. GIT Others agrees with p. 48.

items.head: Levofloxacin dose in the rescue regimen
list: Your book p. 41: “Levofloxacin 500 mg once daily + PPI + Amoxicillin”.
Your book p. 48 and GIT Others p. 5: “levofloxacin 250 or 500 mg twice a day for 10 days” (with PPI + amoxicillin 1 g twice a day).
items.after: Your two pages disagree. GIT Others agrees with p. 48.

items.head: Commonest site of gastric cancer: how common?
list: Your book p. 62: antrum/pyloric area 60%, body 15%, fundus 25%.
GIT Others p. 15: pyloric region 50%, then lesser curvature 25%, but it can occur anywhere in the stomach.
items.after: Both sources agree the pyloric (antral) region is the commonest site. They give different percentages and a different second site.

chapters.title: Pathology of GIT Tumours
chapters.files_note: First-half file, PDF pp. 73–78. Most of GIT Others pp. 13–21 already appears on these pages.

items.fits: Carcinoma of esophagus → Histopathology → 1. Squamous cell carcinoma
items.head: What esophageal SCC looks like under the microscope
text: It is made of islands of neoplastic squamous cells. Differentiated tumours also show epithelial cell nests.

items.fits: Carcinoma of esophagus → effects and complications
items.head: A malignant ulcer can bleed fatally
text: As well as dysphagia and haematemesis, perforation of the malignant ulcer can cause fatal haemorrhage.

items.fits: Gastric adenocarcinoma → Predisposing factors / intestinal type “on top of intestinal metaplasia”
items.head: The H. pylori pathway to gastric cancer
text: H. pylori infection → gastritis → atrophic gastritis → intestinal metaplasia → dysplasia → cancer.
GIT Others calls intestinal metaplasia a precancerous (dysplastic) lesion of the stomach.

items.fits: Gastric adenocarcinoma → “It may take one of two types”
items.head: Name and frequency of the two types
text: The intestinal and diffuse types make up the Lauren classification: intestinal type 53%, diffuse type 33%, unclassified 14%.

items.head: The malignant gastric ulcer
text: The ulcer is typically more than 5 cm across, with an everted edge, a necrotic floor and a firm base.

items.fits: Spread of gastric carcinoma → Blood spread
items.head: Blood spread goes beyond the liver
text: Blood-borne metastases go to the liver and also to the lung, bone and brain.

items.fits: Neoplastic adenomatous polyp of the colon
items.head: Colonic adenomas run in families
text: There is a well-defined familial predisposition to colonic adenomas. They predispose to colorectal carcinoma.

items.head: Tubular vs villous adenoma: size and cancer risk
items.after: GIT Others’ table gives the 40% for adenomas >4 cm; its text gives it for villous adenomas in general.

chapters.title: Foodborn Infection
chapters.files_note: First-half file, PDF pp. 109–117. GIT Others pp. 22–33 repeat these pages almost word for word. Only small laboratory and control details are new.

items.head: Where Salmonella gastroenteritis comes from
text: Poultry are the primary reservoir of Salmonella causing food-borne gastroenteritis. Contaminated eggs are the main food source.

items.head: Salmonella culture and sugar fermentation
list: A facultative anaerobe that grows well at 37 °C in 24 hours. Colonies on MacConkey are pale (yellow) because it does not ferment lactose.
Most species ferment sugars with acid and gas. S. typhi makes acid only (no gas).

items.fits: Enteric fever → Laboratory diagnosis → A. Isolation (first week)
items.head: How the first-week blood culture is done
text: Blood is cultured in fluid (broth) media, then subcultured on solid media, mainly MacConkey, at 37 °C.

items.fits: Enteric fever → Prevention and Control (before “1- Immunization”)
items.head: Control starts with food handlers
text: Food handlers are examined to detect carriers. Carriers are treated or kept away from handling food. GIT Others lists this before immunization.

items.fits: Salmonella food poisoning → A. S. typhimurium
items.head: S. typhimurium food poisoning is self-limiting
text: After lasting 2–5 days, it usually resolves on its own (spontaneous cure).

items.head: Campylobacter laboratory details
list: A rectal swab is an acceptable specimen, collected with care to avoid oxygen exposure.
Darting motility is seen in a wet mount under dark-field illumination.
Isolated colonies are identified by biotyping, serotyping and phage typing.

items.head: Brucella needs CO₂
text: Brucella is aerobic, but culture needs 10% CO₂ as well as serum-enriched media.

items.fits: Enteric fever → Interpretation of Widal test
items.head: Widal test: what a high H titre means
list: Your book p. 109: a high titre to one H antigen (≥1:160) suggests recent infection with that type; high O titre plus more than one H antigen indicates recent immunization.
GIT Others p. 24: “More than one H antigen (≥1:160) suggest recent infection with this type of Salmonella and recent immunization.”
items.after: The GIT Others list here is garbled (its items 1–2 are cut off), so it is not a reliable correction. Ask your teacher before changing what you learned.

items.fits: Familial polyposis coli → “These are adenomatous polyps”
items.head: Polyp type in FAP
text: In FAP, most of the polyps are tubular adenomas.

part_b.checked_none_note: GIT Others also covers Chapter 9 (Parasitic GI Diseases) on pp. 35–47. Every point there is already in your book (pp. 123–138), with the same doses and time periods, so Chapter 9 has no additions.
